overview:
The fighting began in July 1942 as an arm of Case Blue, the German summer offensive aimed at the oil of the Caucasus. Hitler enlarged the objective in late July to include the industrial city on the Volga that carried Stalin's name, and by 23 August the Luftwaffe had bombed much of it into rubble while Friedrich Paulus's Sixth Army closed on the outskirts. What followed was not a campaign of movement but months of house-to-house fighting in factory districts, grain elevators and sewers, with Vasily Chuikov's 62nd Army clinging to a strip of riverbank and feeding reinforcements across the Volga under fire. Stalin's Order No. 227 that summer — "not a step back" — made retreat a punishable offence, and the defence was sustained as much by coercion as by resolve. Civilians were never fully evacuated and died in large numbers in the bombing and the street fighting.

The decisive stroke came on 19 November 1942, when the Red Army launched Operation Uranus, planned under Aleksandr Vasilevsky with Georgy Zhukov and executed on the northern flank by Nikolai Vatutin. Rather than attacking the Germans in the city, the Soviets struck the thinly equipped Romanian Third and Fourth Armies holding the flanks, having concealed the buildup with an elaborate deception effort. The pincers met near Kalach on 22–23 November, sealing roughly a quarter of a million Axis troops in a pocket. Hitler forbade a breakout; an airlift promised by Göring never came close to supplying the trapped army, and Erich von Manstein's December relief attempt stalled short of the ring. Paulus surrendered the remnants on 2 February 1943, the first of Hitler's field armies to capitulate.

The scale of loss is enormous and imprecisely known. Estimates for total casualties run from roughly 800,000 to well over a million on the Soviet side alone, with German losses commonly put in the range of 300,000 to 400,000 and heavy additional casualties among Romanian, Hungarian and Italian formations. Of the Axis prisoners marched into Soviet captivity, only a small fraction ever returned home. The battle also shattered Germany's coalition partners in the east, whose armies were destroyed as effective forces and whose governments began quietly reconsidering their commitment to the war.
significance: Stalingrad ended the strategic initiative that Germany had held on the Eastern Front since 1941, and the Wehrmacht never regained it; from February 1943 onward the war in the east was a long retreat punctuated by counterattacks. Its consequences were psychological as much as military — the surrender of an entire field army punctured the Reich's claim of invincibility, gave the Soviet Union a founding legend of endurance that shaped its self-image for the rest of the century, and reassured Allied governments that the Soviet state would hold. The city itself, destroyed and then rebuilt, became a monument, and "Stalingrad" entered many languages as shorthand for a fight to the last building. Historians still argue whether Moscow, Kursk or Operation Bagration was the truer hinge of the war, but none of them displaced Stalingrad in public memory.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia articles on the battle and on Operation Uranus, a scholarly overview essay from Ohio State's Origins, and Britannica; the dataset itself holds only two events, the August 1942 assault and Uranus, so the intervening months of urban fighting and the German relief and airlift attempts are unrepresented here (and the dataset dates Uranus to 1943 though it opened on 19 November 1942). Casualty figures are genuinely contested rather than merely rounded — Soviet wartime accounting was political, German records for the pocket break off before the surrender, and civilian deaths in the city were never systematically counted.
